note.question: Do autonomous Q-learning pricing algorithms actually learn tacit collusion, or can high prices arise without a collusive equilibrium or meaningful punishment strategy?
note.overview: Two firms repeatedly choose prices in a differentiated Bertrand game while their Q-learning policies respond to the previous price state. The paper formally characterizes (delta, epsilon)-strategy equilibria such as All Defect, Grim Trigger, and Win-Stay-Lose-Shift, and tests whether learned supracompetitive prices actually constitute collusion or a higher-level equilibrium.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: In every discrete period, each algorithm observes the previous price pair, explores with probability epsilon_t or selects a price maximizing its current Q value, firms earn logit-demand profits, and Q values update. This repeats over a finite training run and is evaluated against the firms' discounted infinite-horizon objective. A previous-price state allows an algorithm to condition current prices on a rival's apparent cooperation or deviation. Exploration disrupts punishment strategies and changes which strategy profiles are best responses.
